It's interesting you mention that as we are all taught that wealth can be created thus economics is obviously not zero sum.

Yet when you break it down into its most fundamental component money is little more than a relative measurement of access to finite resources - labor and material. The relative thing is the big part here. Let's say in an economic system with just you and I we both have $100. Well that's exactly the same as if we had $10000000 or $10. We have an identical level of access to goods. But now let's say somehow in the world where we each start with $100 that $1000 of wealth is added and it all goes to me. Now I have $1100 and you have $100. Even though you actually haven't lost anything, your access to finite resources has been dramatically reduced. If we bring Sam into the picture things don't change. Even if we bring Sam and his 7.3 billion friends into the picture it's still the same story.

The thing that I think that economics mixes up is that it conflates technological development with economics. If we're hunter gatherers then we might both be willing to expend large portions of our relative wealth on, for instance, a nice watermelon. But once we've developed formal agriculture a watermelon no longer has as much worth. It's not that you have greater access because of greater wealth, but because technology has effectively reduced the demand for said commodity in this case by increasing the supply, but it can decrease demand in other ways such as for instance by rendering a previously desirable product obsolete.

The belief that the top earning $100 while the bottom earn $1 is still a good thing overall was the fundamental basis for supply side economics. At this point in society I think we can safely say that supply side economics has simply been a failure. Consequently I think it's time to start looking at why it failed, and I've yet to see a rational argument against the above suggesting that economics is indeed effectively zero sum.

To be more subtle, I would argue that economics is not a zero sum game, but is so rigid, it may as well be.

As you point out, money represents access to finite resources. The only resource with any intrinsic value is labor. Gold doesn't actually do anything. Materials are worthless without labor to shape them.

Labor is what produces wealth. With no money, a person could go into the wild, capture animals, build cages, and domesticate the animals for food. They now have more resources than before using nothing but labor.

So what money truly represents is your access to labor. Do I need to build my house myself, or do I pay somebody? Can I grow my business myself, or can I hire?

This means that as population grows, so does wealth. There is more labor to buy, thus there is more wealth in the world. If you create a way to multiply the output of labor (automation) you increase the wealth in the world.

But automation is finite (you can't automate everything) and population growth is also limited. It takes a long time to get from birth to productive adult. So while wealth can grow, making it a non-zero sum game, the amount of wealth at any given time is fixed, as is the rate at which it grows. So it behaves like a zero sum game.

TLDR Your assessment is almost entirely correct, but I believe your argument could be strengthened by accounting for a minor hole in the logic.

But labor and materials aren't zero sum either. The amount of labor has increased with the human population, the quality of that labor has increased with modern education, and similarly the availability and usefulness of materials have increased over time.

Right! But it depends on specific quantities involved. Let's take an example. Let's say there are 10 units of wood available and we both have $100. Well obviously we could both afford to purchase exactly 5 units of wood. Now let's imagine 20 units of wood are made available, perhaps through the invention of a better axe. Well if the relative wealth stays the same then we've both indeed become wealthier as we can both now afford 10 units each when previously we could only afford 5 units each.

But the catch is it that obviously our wealth don't stay the same. They're going to change by some relative amount. In recent times out of every $100 of new income generated $99 of it goes to 1% of the population. So let's grow our example to 100 people to keep the numbers simple. We start with 100 units of wood and each individual having $1 well in this case each person can afford exactly 1 unit of wood. So now let's double the amount of wood available but let's also throw $300 more into the economy. We now have 1 person with $1+$297 = $298 and the everybody else has about $1.02. Well with $400 in the economy and 200 units of wood the price of wood is now $2 a unit meaning nobody except the wealthiest can afford even a single unit. In this case even though technology has doubled the amount of wood available the wealth inequality has actually resulted in nearly everybody being effectively poorer.

And this is what we're seeing in real life as well. Even though our GDP and other macro-scale indicators look amazing actual wages are stagnant to declining. For those that don't understand the graph, the blue line is the median household income in inflation adjusted dollars. In other words more than 50% of Americans are earning less today than they were a decade ago. Even before the recession wages were stagnant. Ultimately our country on paper is becoming vastly wealthier at the same time most of its actual population continue to grow poorer. If economics was not effectively (and I say 'effectively' as there are certainly far more issues than just resource access at work here, but the fundamental issue -more money for some means less for others- remains in play throughout) zero sum this should not be possible.

So I suppose the more accurate phrasing would be that economics becomes zero sum in the presence of extreme levels of wealth inequality.

That's more fair, yes. It's true that ridiculous amounts of wealth inequality can result in most people having less even when more materials are available. However, it's also possible, and indeed much more likely, for everyone to have more even though wealth becomes unequal.

For example, to use your analogy (100 wood units, 100 people, $100), suppose the new axe is invented and as a result the person who invented it is able to sell his invention to loggers everywhere for a major profit to himself. Suppose this causes more than double the wood (200 units), but also causes some inflation such that there are now $109 total dollars (a somewhat more reasonable increase as well, given historical trends). I'll be even more generous and assume that literally 100% of that new money goes to the inventor: now he has $10, but everyone else still has $1.

Here, even though 99% of people now have less relative money, they have more access to materials: their $1 can now buy them almost twice as much wood as it could before, despite the profits of the inventor making him rich enough to afford 19 units himself. As here, in all but the most extreme cases wealth creation does benefit everyone.

What is the best novel published since 2000?

Hmmm tough question. I'll go with Empire Falls by Richard Russo. Normally I'm not a fan of such a sprawling novel but Russo just seems to make it work. I loved the setting, the unhurried feel to it all. The characters were great but for me the town took center stage. I distinctly remember dreading the end, like I didn't want to leave the town of Empire Falls. The books by no means perfect, (I personally didn't enjoy how Russo handled the ending) but I don't think I've read a book published since that has quite stayed with me like Empire Falls has.
Read this a couple of years ago and loved it. The town was a character in itself.

The Name of the Wind by Patrick Rothfuss. Best book I've read in years. Maybe decades. Runner up would be The Martian by Andy Weir. Extremely fast read. It was full of technobabble but it was so fast-paced I barely noticed.
Remainder by Tom Mcarthy. Blew my mind a bit, got me to love reading again.

Jayber Crow by Wendell Berry. Berry was in Wallace Stegner's Stanford writing class along with Larry McMurtry, Edward Abbey, and Ken Kesey. Most of Berry's fiction is set in 20th century rural Kentucky. It chronicles the tumultuous transition from family/community farming to industrial scale agriculture with lots of folk wisdom and humor.
